title: Design "continue where you left off"

titles: System Design: "Continue Where You Left Off" (Save User Progress)
Resume Progress Across Devices: From localStorage to a Million Users
System Design Interview: Save a User's Place When They Close the Tab
publish.description: Forty minutes into a lesson, the tab closes, and you're back on the home page. We design "continue where you left off" the way a real project grows: the URL and local storage for one laptop, progress on the server for many devices, two kinds of session, 20,000 writes per second at the peak, and what to do when two devices disagree. Every piece comes with the problem that asked for it and what it costs.
learn: Why the URL and local storage are the right first answer, and their limits
When to save: why not on unload, and why visibilitychange is the last reliable moment
Moving progress to the server, and the two kinds of session (who you are vs where you were)
Write-heavy math: 200k students saving every 10 s is 20k writes per second
Scaling out a stateless backend, then fixing the database primary: save smarter, partition by student
Out-of-order saves from two devices, and the conditional update that keeps the newest
extra: Browsers don't reliably fire unload or beforeunload, especially on mobile; MDN calls visibilitychange (hidden) the last event that's reliably observable by the page. Send the final save with navigator.sendBeacon (always a POST) or fetch with keepalive.

localStorage survives closing the tab, holds about 5 MiB per origin, is synchronous and stores strings only. Private mode, clearing site data and Safari's 7-day cap on script-writable storage can wipe it.
Return-to-page after login must accept only paths on your own site (OWASP: Unvalidated Redirects and Forwards).
The numbers are our own example: 1M students, 20% watching at 8 pm, one save every 10 s = 20k writes/s; one app open per hour = ~55 reads/s.
publish.comment: What would you have done differently? And which system should I design next?

scenes.heading: Design *continue where you left off*
scenes.subheading: From one laptop to a million students
scenes.narration: Forty minutes into a lesson, halfway through a quiz, the tab closes. You reopen it: home page, empty quiz. How would you design continue where you left off? Start simple, improve it only when needed.

scenes.caption: an online course platform · one laptop each
scenes.narration: Start small. An online course platform with two thousand students. Videos, readings and quizzes, and each student studies on their own laptop.

scenes.title: Before designing
scenes.narration: Before designing: what must it do, and how well? Reopen the app, and you land on the same lesson, at the same second. A half-finished quiz keeps its answers. You lose at most thirty seconds of progress. And resuming adds no visible delay.

scenes.title: What you already have
scenes.narration: Your platform already has the usual pieces. The frontend, the app in the browser. The backend, with its REST API: the backend is everything on your server, the API is its door. And a database with courses and users.

scenes.title: The URL is state
scenes.narration: First idea, and it's free: put where you are in the URL. Lesson seven, minute forty. Refresh, go back or share the link, and you land in the same place. But close the tab and open the site fresh? Home page again.

scenes.title: Local storage
scenes.narration: So the browser remembers it. Local storage is a small key value store inside the browser, and it survives closing the tab. Save the last URL and the quiz draft there. On open, the frontend reads it and jumps straight back. No server change at all.

scenes.title: When to save
scenes.narration: When do you save? Not when the page closes: on phones, that event often never fires. Save as they go: quiz answers a second after the last change, the video position every few seconds. And save when the page gets hidden: that's the last moment you can count on.

steps.note: save(): the URL, the second, the quiz
Not unload: on phones it often never fires
Quiz: 1 s after the last change
Hidden = the last moment you can count on

scenes.title: Is anything else needed?
scenes.narration: For one laptop, is anything else needed? No. No new servers, no new tables, and resuming is instant. The cost: it lives in one browser. Private mode or clearing data wipes it. On a shared computer, key it by user and clear it on logout.

note.text: Shared PC: *key by user, clear on logout*

scenes.caption: laptop at night · phone on the bus
scenes.narration: Now, what if they study on the laptop at night, and continue on the phone on the bus? Does this design hold?

scenes.title: What breaks
scenes.narration: The phone has its own browser, and its own local storage. Empty. Your progress is stuck on a laptop at home. The code isn't the problem. Local storage belongs to a device, and progress belongs to a person.

scenes.title: Progress on the server
scenes.narration: So progress moves to where the person is: your server. A progress table, one row per student and course: the lesson, the second, the quiz answers, and when it was saved. On open, any device asks the API for it.

scenes.title: Saving over the network
scenes.narration: While they watch, the frontend saves the position every ten seconds. When the page gets hidden, it sends one last save as a beacon: a small request the browser keeps sending even as the page goes away.

note.text: Sent by the browser, *not the page*

scenes.title: What it costs
scenes.narration: The cost: a write every ten seconds per active student. At two thousand students, that's at most two hundred a second: one database is plenty. The server takes the student from the login, never from the request. If the network fails, keep the local copy and send it later.

note.text: Student *from the login*, not the request

scenes.title: The login expires
scenes.narration: And if they just stop using the app for two hours? The login session expires, on purpose, for security. They log back in, and the login page sends everyone home. Progress is saved; the redirect forgot it.

scenes.title: Two kinds of session
scenes.narration: The word session hides two things. Like a hotel: your key card expires, your stored luggage doesn't. Who you are should expire. Where you were should not. After login, send them back to the page they asked for. Only paths on your own site, or attackers can abuse it.

scenes.caption: say 200k watching at once at 8 pm
scenes.narration: The platform grows. One million students, and at eight in the evening, say two hundred thousand are watching at once. Does it hold?

scenes.title: Do the math
scenes.narration: Do the math first. Two hundred thousand students, a save every ten seconds: twenty thousand writes per second. Reads only happen when someone opens the app: a few dozen per second. This system is almost all writes.

scenes.title: Scale out first
scenes.narration: The standard first step: a load balancer, which spreads requests over several copies of your backend. That works because the backend is stateless: it keeps nothing between requests. Progress lives in the database, not in a server's memory, so any copy can take any save.

scenes.title: Where it moved
scenes.narration: But every copy writes to the same database. Its primary, the one copy that accepts writes, takes every save. The load grows with every student, and you can't just copy it. A read cache or replicas won't help: this is writes.

note.text: Primary = *the one server that accepts writes*

scenes.title: Save smarter
scenes.narration: The cheap fix first. Your requirement allows losing thirty seconds, so use that budget. Save every thirty seconds, plus on pause, on lesson change and when the page is hidden. About a third of the writes. The cost: if the browser crashes, they lose up to thirty seconds.

note.text: Cost: up to *30 s* lost on a crash

scenes.title: A store built for writes
scenes.narration: If saves outgrow one primary, move progress to a database built for small writes by key: DynamoDB, Cassandra, or Redis with persistence on. Or split Postgres by student. Either way, each save touches one partition, and no single student is a hot spot.

scenes.title: What it costs
scenes.narration: The cost: one more database to run and back up. And questions across students, like how many finished lesson three, get hard there. Send those as events to your analytics, and keep the main database for courses, users and payments.

scenes.caption: the phone and the laptop both save progress
scenes.narration: One last question. The phone and the laptop both save progress. Which one wins?

scenes.title: Out of order
scenes.narration: On the bus, the phone has no signal, so its saves wait. At home, the laptop moves you on to lesson four. Then the phone reconnects and sends lesson three, from an hour ago. The last save to arrive wins, so lesson three wins. You go back an hour.

note.text: Last to arrive wins → *you go back*

scenes.title: Keep the newest
scenes.narration: The fix: every save carries when it happened. The store keeps it only if it's newer than what it has, in one atomic step: check and write together. A late save is ignored. The cost: device clocks can be wrong, so some apps ask: lesson four, or lesson three?

note.text: Clocks can be wrong → *ask the user*

scenes.title: When is local enough?
scenes.narration: Careful: none of this is always needed. One device, no accounts, a form draft? Local storage is enough. Progress that follows a person across devices? That's the server. And when saves outgrow one primary, a store built for writes.

items.text: Saves outgrow one primary → *a write store*

scenes.title: The path
scenes.narration: Look at the path. We started with the URL and local storage, and each piece came when a real problem asked for it. Another device: the server. Millions: save smarter and split by student. Two devices: keep the newest. What would you have done differently?
scenes.cta: What would you have done differently?

scenes.title: Before you go
scenes.narration: Leave your answer in the comments, and tell me which system we design next: a URL shortener, a chat, or a payment system. If this helped, a like and a subscribe help the channel a lot. See you in the next one.

notes: In an interview, ask first: one device or many? Logged in or anonymous? How much progress can you lose? How many students at the peak? Those four answers pick the design.

URL first: anything that defines where you are (lesson, tab, filters, page of results) belongs in the URL, because refresh, back, bookmarks and shared links then work for free. Local storage only remembers which URL was last.

Storage in the browser: sessionStorage is per tab and gone when it closes; localStorage is per origin, survives restarts, about 5 MiB, synchronous and strings only; IndexedDB is async and much bigger, for offline-first apps. Private mode, clearing site data and Safari's 7-day cap on script-writable storage (after 7 days of Safari use without interacting with the site) can wipe it: it is a convenience, not a source of truth.

Why not save on unload or beforeunload: browsers don't guarantee those events, especially on mobile, where apps are backgrounded and killed without closing. MDN calls visibilitychange (hidden) the last event that's reliably observable by the page. Unload handlers also break the back/forward cache.

Beacon details: navigator.sendBeacon always sends a POST and can't set custom headers (auth goes in the cookie), so the endpoint must accept POST; fetch with keepalive allows PUT and headers, with a body limit of about 64 KiB.
Shared computers: key the local copy by user id and clear it on logout, so the next person never sees someone else's lesson or quiz answers.

Why not keep progress in the server's session memory: that makes the backend stateful. With several copies you need sticky sessions, and a restart or deploy loses it. Progress is data; it belongs in a database.

Two kinds of session: the auth session (a cookie or token) should expire for security; the work state should not. After login, redirect to the saved return path, but accept only relative paths on your own site (OWASP Unvalidated Redirects and Forwards: otherwise attackers send users to a phishing page with your domain in the link). Two hours idle is our example; OWASP suggests shorter idle timeouts for many apps.

The math (our own example): 1M students, 20% watching at 8 pm = 200k; one save every 10 s = 20k writes/s; one app open per hour = ~55 reads/s. Data is small (~1 KB per row with a quiz draft, 1M × 5 courses ≈ 5 GB). The problem is write rate, not size, which is why a read cache and read replicas don't help.

A single tuned Postgres primary can take thousands of small updates per second; whether 20k/s fits depends on hardware and indexes. The point is that it is the one piece that doesn't scale by adding copies, and the load grows with every student. Before changing databases, save less: it is free.

Write-heavy options: Redis with AOF persistence (fsync everysec can lose about one second on a crash, inside the 30 s budget; flushing to Postgres later is write-behind), DynamoDB (managed, partitioned by key, pay per write), Cassandra (built for heavy writes; Netflix has written about using it for viewing history), or Postgres partitioned by student id. Partition key = student: no single student is hot.

Conflicts: last write wins is simple but wrong when saves arrive late. A conditional update (UPDATE ... WHERE saved_at < :new) keeps the newest in one atomic step. In DynamoDB it is a condition expression; in Redis a Lua script; in Cassandra a conditional write is a lightweight transaction (Paxos, several round trips), so the cheap way is writing with USING TIMESTAMP = saved_at. Device clocks drift: use server time for online saves, client time only for queued offline saves, or keep the furthest point per lesson. On opening the app, local copy vs server copy: same rule, newest wins.

Abuse: the server takes the user id from the session, never from the request body (otherwise anyone can overwrite someone else's progress: an IDOR). Rate limit PUT /progress per user. If progress unlocks certificates, the position the client sends can't be trusted: validate watched time on the server.

Follow-ups an interviewer may ask: how long do you keep progress (forever, it is tiny)? Deleting an account (delete the rows)? How do you know saves are failing (alert on the error rate of PUT /progress)? Offline mode (an IndexedDB queue that syncs on reconnect)?
